analogy.p: Think of a manager sending a report to an overseas office. The manager writes the report (application), the post room splits it into numbered envelopes (transport), the shipping department writes the full address on each (internet), and the courier van actually carries them along the road (link). At the other end the layers run backwards: the van delivers, the shipping department checks the address, the post room puts the pages in order and the manager reads it. If the firm swaps vans for lorries, the manager does not have to change how they write reports, just as swapping Wi-Fi for Ethernet does not change the browser. The analogy breaks down because in a real network each layer adds a header to the data as it passes down, and real packets are not handled by people.

bullets: A **layer** is a group of protocols that carries out one defined job in network communication.
The J277 model has **four layers**: **Application, Transport, Internet, Link** (from top to bottom).
The Internet layer is sometimes called the Network layer, and the Link layer is sometimes called the Network access or Data link layer.
Each layer uses the services of the layer below and provides services to the layer above.
Layers are **self-contained**: a layer does its job without needing to know how the others do theirs.
Memory aid for top to bottom: **A T**idy **I**nternet **L**ink (**A**pplication, **T**ransport, **I**nternet, **L**ink).
core.p: Sending data across a network is a complicated job: the data must be prepared for the user's program, split up, addressed, routed and finally turned into electrical, light or radio signals. Instead of one huge set of rules doing everything, networking splits the job into **layers**. Each layer has its own clearly defined task and only talks to the layer directly above and below it. OCR J277 uses the **four-layer TCP/IP model**: **application, transport, internet and link**. The concept of layers is a way of breaking a large problem into smaller, self-contained parts.

bullets: Closest to the **user and their software** (browser, email client, FTP client).
Protocols here include **HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP and IMAP**.
It decides **what kind of conversation** is happening: web page, file transfer, sending or collecting email.
It **formats the data** according to the protocol and passes it to the transport layer.
On the receiving side it hands the finished data to the program that will display it.
Exam tip: if a question names HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP or IMAP, the layer is **application**.
core.p: The **application layer** is the layer closest to the user. Programs such as a web browser or an email client use it to start communication, and it holds the protocols that define how those programs exchange data. It takes the user's request (for example 'show me this web page' or 'send this email') and prepares the data in the format the chosen protocol needs, then passes it down to the transport layer.

bullets: Main protocol: **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol).
**Splits data into packets** at the sender and **reassembles** them at the receiver.
**Numbers** each packet so they can be put in order.
**Error checking** and acknowledgements: lost or damaged packets are requested again.
Uses **port numbers** to pass data to the right application on the receiving device.
Gives the layer above the impression of a **reliable** connection even though the network below is not perfectly reliable.
core.p: The **transport layer** is responsible for managing the delivery of the data between the two devices. The main protocol is **TCP**. At the sending end TCP splits the data into **packets** and gives each one a **packet number** (and a port number that identifies which application should receive it). At the receiving end it checks that every packet has arrived, asks for any lost or damaged packet to be resent, and puts the packets back into the correct order.

bullets: Main protocol: **IP** (Internet Protocol).
Adds the **source and destination IP addresses** to each packet.
**Routers** use the destination address to choose the next step (**routing**).
Allows packets to cross many different networks, using **packet switching**.
Does not worry about whether the packet arrives; reliability is handled by TCP in the layer above.
Exam tip: 'which layer adds IP addresses?' is the **internet layer**.
core.p: The **internet layer** deals with addressing and routing across the whole network. The main protocol is **IP** (Internet Protocol). It adds the **source IP address** and **destination IP address** to each packet. **Routers** work with these addresses to forward each packet, hop by hop, towards its destination, which is how **packet switching** works. This layer is what allows data to move between different networks, not just within one local network.

bullets: Lowest layer; handles the **physical connection** between neighbouring devices.
Standards: **Ethernet** (wired) and **Wi-Fi** (wireless); Bluetooth is another short-range wireless link.
Converts data into **electrical, light or radio signals** suited to the transmission medium.
Uses the hardware address (**MAC address**) of the **network interface card** to deliver to the next device on the same link.
Only moves data **one hop**, from one device to the next; the internet layer plans the whole journey.
Exam tip: if the question mentions Ethernet, Wi-Fi or cables, the layer is **link**.
core.p: The **link layer** is the lowest layer. It deals with the physical connection between two directly connected devices, such as your laptop and your router. It turns the data into signals that suit the medium (electrical signals in copper, light in fibre or radio waves in Wi-Fi) and sends them across that one link. Standards such as **Ethernet** and **Wi-Fi** work here. On arrival it passes the data up to the internet layer. The network interface card in each device works at this layer.

bullets: Order for sending: **application, transport, internet, link**.
Each layer **adds a header** containing the information that layer needs.
Transport header: packet number and port; internet header: **IP addresses**; link header: the address of the next device.
Wrapping the data like this is called **encapsulation**.
The result is a stream of signals on the cable or radio waves.
Think of putting a letter in an envelope, then in a bigger parcel, then in a sack: each layer adds a wrapper.
core.h: Sending data: going down the layers
core.p: When you send data, it travels **down** the layers on your device. The application layer prepares the message, the transport layer splits it into numbered packets, the internet layer adds the IP addresses and the link layer sends it out as signals. As data passes down, each layer adds its own information, called a **header**, around the data it has received. This wrapping-up is called **encapsulation**. The link layer may also add a trailer for error checking.

bullets: Order for receiving: **link, internet, transport, application** (bottom to top).
Each layer **removes its own header** (decapsulation) and passes the rest up.
Transport reassembles the packets using the **packet numbers** and requests any missing ones.
The application layer gives the finished data to the **browser or email program**.
Each layer works with its **matching layer** on the other device, using the same protocol.
If any packet is missing the transport layer notices and asks for it again.
core.h: Receiving data: going up the layers
core.p: At the receiving device the process is reversed. The link layer receives the signals and rebuilds the data, the internet layer checks the IP address and removes its header, the transport layer reassembles the packets in the correct order and checks for missing ones, and the application layer hands the complete message to the program that needs it. Each layer removes only the header that its partner layer added.

bullets: Application: **SMTP** formats the email for sending.
Transport: **TCP** splits it into numbered **packets**.
Internet: **IP** adds the **IP addresses**; routers forward the packets.
Link: **Wi-Fi/Ethernet** sends the signals to the next device.
At the receiver: link, internet, transport, application, so the message is **reassembled** and displayed.
Always write the layers in the correct order and say what each one does.
core.h: Worked example: an email across the layers
core.p: To see the model working, follow an email. Application layer: the email client uses SMTP to prepare the message. Transport layer: TCP splits it into numbered packets. Internet layer: IP adds the source and destination addresses so routers can forward the packets. Link layer: Wi-Fi or Ethernet turns the packets into signals and sends them to the router. At the destination the layers run in reverse order and the recipient's email program shows the message.

bullets: **Application**: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP, IMAP.
**Transport**: TCP (splits, numbers, checks, reassembles).
**Internet**: IP (addresses and routing).
**Link**: Ethernet, Wi-Fi (and other physical connection standards such as Bluetooth).
One protocol may rely on those in the layers beneath it; for example HTTPS depends on TCP and IP.
Do not place TCP and IP in the same layer; they have different jobs.
core.h: Which protocol belongs to which layer
core.p: A common exam task is to sort protocols into layers. The rule is that protocols concerned with what the user is doing (web pages, email, files) are application layer protocols, TCP is the transport layer, IP is the internet layer, and the standards for physical connections are link layer. Learning this one table gives you easy marks.

bullets: Breaks a **complex problem into smaller, manageable parts**.
A layer can be **changed or improved without affecting the others** (e.g. swap Ethernet for Wi-Fi).
Different teams or companies can work on different layers at the same time.
Layers follow **standards**, so products from different manufacturers are compatible.
Makes **fault finding** easier because the problem can be traced to one layer.
Easier to teach, understand and develop new protocols.
core.p: Layers are used because they make networks easier to design, improve and repair. As each layer is self-contained, designers can change or upgrade one layer without having to change the others. This is why you can move from a cable to Wi-Fi without changing your browser. Layers also let different companies build hardware and software to common standards, and they help engineers find faults.

bullets: Each layer adds a **header**, which adds a small amount of **extra data** (overhead).
Passing through every layer takes **processing time**.
A fault in one layer can stop communication even if the other layers work.
A change to the way two layers pass data to each other (the interface) can affect both.
The model is a **simplified description**, and real systems may blur the layers.
Exam answers should still stress that the advantages outweigh these.
core.p: Layering is not free. Each layer adds its own header, so the total amount of data sent is larger than the message alone, and passing the data through several layers takes a small amount of processing time. These costs are normally small, and the benefits of standard, self-contained layers outweigh them. It is also important to remember that the model is a simplified description of what really happens.

bullets: Packet switching: **routers** work using IP addresses (internet layer).
Reassembly and numbering: **TCP** (transport layer).
HTTPS is an **application layer** protocol that encrypts the web data before it travels across the network.
Wired and wireless connections: the **link layer**.
Network security threats such as interception happen on the physical link, which is why HTTPS matters.
Use layer names as headings to structure a long answer.
core.h: Link to packet switching and protocols
core.p: The layer ideas connect the whole of section 1.3. Packet switching is done by the internet layer (routers read IP addresses), and TCP at the transport layer makes sure the packets are reassembled. The protocols you learned, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP and IMAP, are the application layer. Ethernet and Wi-Fi are the link layer. If you can place each protocol in its layer you can explain almost any networking question.

bullets: **Network interface card (NIC)** and switches: link layer.
**Routers**: internet layer, choosing the next hop from the destination IP address.
**Browsers and email clients**: application layer.
Each device only needs to understand the layers it works at.
This is why upgrading a router does not require you to change your browser.
Extension only: not required for the J277 exam, but useful for high-mark explanations.
core.p: Different network devices work at different layers. A switch and the network interface card use link layer addresses to deliver data within one local network, while a router works at the internet layer, using IP addresses to forward packets between networks. A web browser is an application. This is beyond what the J277 specification requires, but it shows why the layers matter.

exam: Learn the order and say it every time: **application, transport, internet, link**.
'Name the layer' questions (1 mark): match the protocol or job (HTTPS and SMTP application; TCP transport; IP internet; Ethernet and Wi-Fi link).
'Describe what happens at the transport layer' (2 marks): data is split into packets, numbered and reassembled at the destination, with error checking.
'Explain one advantage of layers' (2 marks): a point plus a reason, e.g. 'each layer is self-contained so one layer can be changed without affecting the others'.
For 4 mark questions about sending data, work down the layers in order and give one clear job for each.
Mention **packets, IP addresses, headers, signals** as key terms.
If asked for 'two advantages', give two different ideas (e.g. compatibility from standards; easier fault finding).
Do not confuse the TCP/IP four-layer model with other layer models with more layers; use the four layers named in J277.
In scenario questions, link the layer to the example (e.g. 'the transport layer splits the photo into packets').
Receiving is the reverse of sending; say that data moves up the layers.

mistakes.r: Top to bottom: application, transport, internet, link.
mistakes.w: Putting the layers in the wrong order.

mistakes.r: HTTP is application layer; TCP is transport layer.
mistakes.w: HTTP and TCP are in the same layer.

mistakes.r: The transport layer (TCP) splits the data into packets; the internet layer adds the IP addresses.
mistakes.w: The internet layer splits data into packets.

mistakes.r: Routing is the internet layer; the link layer only moves data between neighbouring devices.
mistakes.w: The link layer chooses the route across the internet.

mistakes.r: Layers make networks easier to design, change, standardise and fix; they do not make it faster.
mistakes.w: Layers are used to make the network faster.

mistakes.r: It is the layer of protocols the program uses, such as HTTP or SMTP.
mistakes.w: The application layer means the program itself.

mistakes.r: When receiving, data goes up: link, internet, transport, application.
mistakes.w: When receiving, data goes down the layers.

mistakes.r: Explain the result: a layer can be changed without affecting the others.
mistakes.w: Just saying 'it is self-contained' with no explanation.

summary: OCR J277 1.3 asks you to describe the concept of layers and the four layers of the TCP/IP model (application, transport, internet and link), say what each layer does and which protocols belong in it, and explain why layering is used. It matters because Paper 1 asks you to place protocols in layers, trace data through the layers and justify the use of layers.

terms.d: A group of protocols that carries out one defined part of network communication.
A four-layer model of network communication: application, transport, internet and link.
The layer containing protocols used by programs such as web browsers and email clients, e.g. HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP, IMAP.
The layer that splits data into packets, numbers them, checks for errors and reassembles them; uses TCP.
The layer that adds IP addresses to packets and routes them across networks; uses IP.
The layer that sends data across the physical connection between two directly connected devices, e.g. using Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
A set of rules that allows devices to communicate.
A small unit of data sent across a network, with header information, data and error checking.
Extra information (such as addresses and packet number) added to the front of data by a layer.
Wrapping data with headers as it passes down the layers.
A number identifying a device on a network, used by the internet layer for routing.
A hardware address of a network interface card, used on the link layer to deliver data to the next device.
A device that forwards packets between networks using IP addresses.
The hardware that connects a device to a network and sends and receives signals.
Able to do its job without depending on how other layers work.

worked.q: State the layer at which each of the following is used: (a) HTTPS (b) IP (c) Wi-Fi (d) TCP. [4 marks]
steps: HTTPS is a protocol used by a browser, so application layer.
IP adds addresses and routes packets, so internet layer.
Wi-Fi is a standard for the physical wireless connection, so link layer.
TCP splits data into packets and reassembles them, so transport layer.

worked.ans: At the application layer the email client uses SMTP to prepare the email for sending. At the transport layer TCP splits it into numbered packets. At the internet layer IP adds the source and destination IP addresses so routers can forward the packets. At the link layer the packets are turned into signals (for example by Wi-Fi) and sent to the next device.
worked.q: Describe what happens to an email as it is sent from a laptop using the four-layer TCP/IP model. [4 marks]
steps: Then transport, internet and link in order.
One clear job for each layer.

worked.ans: Each layer is self-contained, so a layer can be changed or upgraded (such as swapping Ethernet for Wi-Fi) without having to change the other layers. Layers follow agreed standards, so hardware and software made by different manufacturers can work together.
worked.q: Explain two advantages of using layers in network communication. [4 marks]
steps: Advantage 1: self-contained so one layer can be changed without affecting the others.
Advantage 2: standard so products from different manufacturers work together, or easier fault finding.
Add a consequence to each to gain the second mark.
